source_text: Τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα, πρόσκαιρα, τὰ δὲ μὴ βλεπόμενα, αἰώνια. Ὃ δὲ λέγει τοιοῦτόν ἐστι· Μάλιστα μὲν οὖν καὶ ἐνταῦθα ἡμᾶς ὀνίνησιν ἡ θλῖψις, σοφωτέραν ἡμῶν ποιοῦσα τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ φιλοσοφωτέραν· μετὰ δὲ τοῦτο καὶ μυρία ἡμῖν προξενεῖ κατὰ τὸ μέλλον ἀγαθὰ, οὐκ ἀντίῤῥοπα τῶν πόνων, ἀλλὰ πολλῷ μείζονα τῶν παλαισμάτων καὶ κατὰ τὴν ποσότητα καὶ κατὰ τὴν ποιότητα. Ταῦτα ἀμφότερα, λέγω, δηλῶν ὁ Παῦλος, καὶ τὴν ὑπεροχὴν τῶν κινδύνων, καὶ τῶν ἄθλων ποιεῖται τὴν σύγκρισιν, καὶ ἀντιτίθησι τῷ παραυτίκα τὸ αἰώνιον, τῷ ἐλαφρῷ τὸ βάρος, τῇ θλίψει τὴν δόξαν. Ἡ μὲν γὰρ θλῖψις πρόσκαιρος, φησὶ, καὶ κούφη, ἡ δὲ ἄνεσις μᾶλλον δὲ οὐκ εἶπεν, ἄνεσις, ἀλλὰ, δόξα, ὃ πολλῷ μεῖζον τῆς ἀνέσεως αἰώνιος καὶ διηνεκὴς καὶ μεγάλη. Βάρος δὲ ἐνταῦθα, οὐ τὸ ἐπίπονον καὶ φορτικὸν εἶπεν, ἀλλὰ τὸ πολυτελὲς καὶ ἔντιμον, κατὰ τὸ τῶν πολλῶν ἔθος, οἳ τὰ πολύτιμα οὕτω καὶ βαρύτιμα κα50.425 λεῖν εἰώθασιν. Ὅταν οὖν εἴπῃ βάρος δόξης, μέγεθος δόξης λέγει. Μὴ τοίνυν τοῦτο μόνον λογίζου, φησὶν, ὅτι μαστίζῃ καὶ ἐλαύνῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς στεφάνους καὶ τὰς ἀμοιβὰς, ὅτι πολλῷ μείζους καὶ λαμπρότεραι τῶν παρόντων ἐκεῖναι, καὶ τέλος οὐκ ἔχουσιν, οὐδὲ πέρας. Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα, φησὶν, ἐν πείρᾳ, ἐκεῖνα δὲ ἐν ἐλπίσι· καὶ ταῦτα μὲν φανερὰ, ἐκεῖνα δὲ οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλ' ἐκκρεμῆ καὶ μετέωρά εἰσιν· ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ ἀφανῆ, ἀλλὰ τῶν φαινομένων ἐστὶ φανερώτερα. Τί λέγω φανερώτερα; Ἐκεῖνα δύνασαι μᾶλλον ὁρᾷν, ἢ ταῦτα. Ταῦτα μὲν γὰρ παρέρχεται, ἐκεῖνα δὲ μένει. Διὸ ἐπήγαγε, λέγων· Μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα· τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα πρόσκαιρα, τὰ δὲ μὴ βλεπόμενα αἰώνια. εʹ. Εἰ δὲ λέγοις· Καὶ πῶς δυνήσομαι τὰ ἀφανῆ βλέπειν, τὰ δὲ παρόντα μὴ βλέπειν; ἀπὸ τῶν βιωτικῶν σε εἰς ταύτην ἐναγαγεῖν πειράσομαι τὴν πίστιν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ πραγμάτων τῶν ἐπικήρων τούτων ἅψαιτό τις ἂν ῥᾳδίως, μὴ τὰ ἀφανῆ πρὸ τῶν φανερῶν ἰδών. Οἷόν τι λέγω· Ὁ ἔμπορος ὑπομένει μὲν χειμῶνας πολλοὺς καὶ κυμάτων ἐπαναστάσεις καὶ ναυάγια καὶ μυρίας δυσκολίας, ἀπολαύει δὲ καὶ πλούτου μετὰ τοὺς χειμῶνας, τὰ φορτία διατιθέμενος, καὶ πολλὴν ἐργαζόμενος πραγματείαν. Ἀλλ' οἱ μὲν χειμῶνες πρότεροι, τὰ δὲ φορτία ὕστερα· καὶ τὰ μὲν πελάγη καὶ τὰ κύματα φαίνεται ἐξελθόντι τοῦ λιμένος, ἡ ἐμπορία δὲ οὐ φαίνεται· ἐν ἐλπίσι γάρ ἐστιν ἔτι. Ἀλλ' ὅμως ἂν μὴ πρὸς ἐκείνην ἴδῃ πρῶτον τὴν ἀφανῆ καὶ μὴ παροῦσαν, μηδὲ ἐν χερσὶν οὖσαν, ἀλλ' ἐν ἐλπίσιν, οὐκ ἂν ἅψαιτο τούτων τῶν παρόντων καὶ φαινομένων. Οὕτω καὶ γεωργὸς ζεύγνυσι βόας, καὶ ἄροτρον ἕλκει, καὶ βαθεῖαν αὔλακα ἀνατέμνει, καὶ σπέρματα καταβάλλει, καὶ τὰ ὄντα ἅπαντα δαπανᾷ, καὶ κρυμὸν καὶ πάγον καὶ ὄμβρους καὶ ἑτέρας ἀνέχεται ταλαιπωρίας πολλὰς, καὶ μετὰ τὸν πόνον τοῦτον προσδοκᾷ κομῶντα ὄψεσθαι τὰ λήϊα, καὶ πεπληρωμένην τὴν ἅλωνα. Ὁρᾷς πῶς καὶ ἐνταῦθα πρότερος ὁ πόνος, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ μισθός· καὶ ὁ μὲν μισθὸς ἄδηλος, ὁ δὲ πόνος δῆλος καὶ φανερός· κἀκεῖνος μὲν ἐν ἐλπίσιν, οὗτος δὲ ἐν χερσίν; Ἀλλ' ὅμως καὶ οὗτος ἂν μὴ πρότερον πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ἴδῃ τὸν ἄδηλον καὶ ἀφανῆ καὶ μὴ βλεπόμενον τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς τοῦ σώματος μισθὸν, οὐ μόνον οὐ ζεύξει βόας, οὐδὲ ἄροτρον ἕλξει, οὐδὲ σπέρματα καταβαλεῖ, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ κινηθήσεται οἴκοθεν πρὸς τὴν ἐργασίαν ταύτην ποτέ.
thought_title: The Unseen Is More Certain Than the Seen
orientation: Chrysostom is expounding Paul's words in 2 Corinthians 4:17-18, explaining why affliction is light and momentary compared with the eternal weight of glory, and why believers must look at unseen things.
pass_a_gloss: For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. What he says is something like this: Most of all, then, affliction benefits us even here, making our soul wiser and more philosophical; and after this it also procures for us countless good things in the future, not equal in weight to the labors, but much greater than the wrestling matches both in quantity and in quality. Paul, I say, making clear both of these things, makes the comparison of the superiority of the prizes over the dangers, and he sets against the momentary the eternal, against the light the weight, against the affliction the glory. For the affliction, he says, is temporary and light, but the relief—rather, he did not say relief, but glory, which is much greater than relief—is eternal and perpetual and great. By weight here he did not mean the laborious and burdensome, but the costly and honored, according to the custom of the many, who are accustomed to call very precious things also very weighty. Whenever, then, he says weight of glory, he means greatness of glory. Do not, then, he says, consider only this, that you are scourged and driven, but also the crowns and the rewards, that those are much greater and more splendid than the present things, and they have no end, nor limit. But these things, he says, are in experience, but those are in hopes; and these things are visible, but those do not appear, but are suspended and in mid-air; but even if they are unseen, they are more visible than the things that appear. Why do I say more visible? You are able to see those more than these. For these things pass away, but those remain. Therefore he added, saying: While we look not at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. 5. But if you should say: And how will I be able to see the unseen things, and not to see the present things? I will try to lead you from the affairs of life into this faith. For no one would readily touch even the perishable affairs of this world, unless he first saw the unseen things before the visible things. I mean something like this: The merchant endures many storms and risings of waves and shipwrecks and countless difficulties, and he also enjoys wealth after the storms, disposing of the cargoes and carrying on much trade. But the storms come first, and the cargoes later; and the seas and the waves are seen by him when he has gone out of the harbor, but the trade is not seen; for it is still in hopes. But nevertheless, unless he first looks to that unseen thing which is not present, nor in his hands, but in hopes, he would not touch these present and visible things. So also the farmer yokes oxen, and drags the plow, and cuts a deep furrow, and casts down seeds, and spends all his possessions, and endures frost and ice and rains and many other hardships, and after this labor he expects to see the crops flourishing and the threshing floor filled. Do you see how here too the labor comes first, and after this the reward; and the reward is uncertain, but the labor is clear and visible; and that one is in hopes, but this one is in his hands? But nevertheless, this man too, unless he first looks to that uncertain and unseen reward, not seen by the eyes of the body, not only will he not yoke oxen, nor drag the plow, nor cast down seeds, but he will not even be moved from his house to this work ever.

choices.term: ὑπεροχὴν τῶν κινδύνων, καὶ τῶν ἄθλων ποιεῖται τὴν σύγκρισιν
choices.english: makes the comparison of the superiority of the prizes over the dangers
choices.why: The genitive phrase indicates the prizes' superiority over the dangers, not the reverse; Paul compares how the prizes exceed the dangers.
rejected: he compares how the dangers exceed the prizes

choices.why: Chrysostom explicitly reinterprets Paul's 'weight' as costly and honored, not burdensome; keeping 'weight' preserves the Pauline term while the gloss explains it.
Chrysostom contrasts what Paul did not say (relief) with what he did say (glory); 'relief' captures the ordinary term Paul avoided.
The two adjectives describe the unseen things as hanging in the air, not yet grasped; the literal rendering preserves the vivid spatial metaphor.
The verb means to bring or lead into; 'lead you into this faith' preserves the directional force of the prefix.
The noun means a rising up; 'risings of waves' keeps the literal sense of waves rising against the merchant.

bible_refs.note: τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα πρόσκαιρα, τὰ δὲ μὴ βλεπόμενα αἰώνια
Μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα

pass_b_english: For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18). What he means is this: affliction benefits us most of all even here, making our soul wiser and more philosophical, and after this it also procures for us countless good things in the age to come—not merely counterbalancing our labors, but far greater than our wrestling matches, both in quantity and in quality. Paul makes both of these points clear, I say, and he compares the surpassing greatness of the dangers and the prizes, setting the eternal against the momentary, the weight against the light, the glory against the affliction. For affliction, he says, is temporary and light, but the relief—or rather he did not say relief, but glory, which is far greater than relief—is eternal and perpetual and great. By weight here he does not mean what is burdensome and heavy to carry, but what is costly and honored, according to the custom of most people, who are accustomed to call very valuable things very weighty. So when he says weight of glory, he means greatness of glory. Do not think only of this, he says—that you are scourged and driven about—but also of the crowns and the rewards, because those are far greater and more splendid than the present things, and they have no end and no limit. But these things, he says, are in trial, while those are in hopes; and these are visible, while those do not appear but are suspended and in mid-air. Yet even if they are unseen, they are more visible than the things that are seen. What do I mean, more visible? You can see those things more than these. For these things pass away, but those remain. That is why he added: While we look not at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Corinthians 4:18). But if you say, How will I be able to see the unseen things and not see the present things? I will try to lead you into this faith from the affairs of daily life. For no one would readily lay hold of even the perishable affairs of this world without first seeing the unseen things before the visible ones. What I mean is this: the merchant endures many storms and risings of waves and shipwrecks and countless difficulties, and he also enjoys wealth after the storms, disposing of his cargo and carrying on much business. But the storms come first, and the cargo comes later; and the seas and the waves are visible when he leaves the harbor, but the trade is not visible, for it is still in hopes. Yet unless he first looks to that unseen thing which is not present and not in his hands but in hopes, he would not lay hold of these present and visible things. So also the farmer yokes oxen, drags the plow, cuts a deep furrow, casts in seed, spends all that he has, and endures frost and ice and rains and many other hardships; and after this labor he expects to see the fields thick with grain and the threshing floor filled. Do you see how here too the labor comes first, and after it the reward—and the reward is unseen, while the labor is clear and visible; and the one is in hopes, while the other is in his hands? Yet unless he first looks to that reward which is unseen and invisible and not visible to the eyes of the body, he will not only not yoke oxen or drag the plow or cast in seed, but he will never even stir from his house to go to this work.

problems.quote: not equal in weight to our labors
problems.why: ἀντίρροπος means 'counterbalancing' or 'equivalent,' not 'equal in weight to'—the point is rewards exceed labors, not that they're unequal in weight.

problems.quote: the comparison of the superiority of the prizes over the dangers
problems.source_quote: τῶν κινδύνων, καὶ τῶν ἄθλων ποιεῖται τὴν σύγκρισιν
problems.why: Source says he compares dangers AND prizes; English says 'superiority of prizes over dangers,' dropping the comparison of both.
problems.fix: and he compares the dangers and the prizes
problems.ruling: Greek has 'comparison of dangers and prizes' (τῶν κινδύνων, καὶ τῶν ἄθλων); English reverses to 'superiority of prizes over dangers,' misrepresenting Paul's balanced comparison.

problems.quote: But these things, he says, are in experience
problems.source_quote: Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα, φησὶν, ἐν πείρᾳ, ἐκεῖνα δὲ ἐν ἐλπίσιν
problems.why: ἐν πείρᾳ means 'in trial/testing/suffering,' not 'in experience'—contrasts present suffering with future hope.
problems.fix: But these things, he says, are in trial
problems.ruling: ἐν πείρᾳ means 'in trial/suffering'; 'in experience' misleads, losing the contrast with ἐν ἐλπίσι ('in hopes').

problems.why: ἄδηλος means 'unseen/not manifest,' not 'uncertain'—the farmer's hope is sure though invisible, not doubtful.
problems.ruling: ἄδηλος means 'unseen/not manifest'; 'uncertain' introduces doubt, changing the theological point about sure but invisible hope.

problems.quote: that reward which is uncertain and unseen
problems.why: Same error: ἄδηλος is 'unseen,' not 'uncertain'—changes the theological point about faith in unseen realities.
problems.fix: that reward which is unseen and invisible
problems.ruling: ἄδηλος means 'unseen/not manifest'; 'uncertain' wrongly implies doubt, altering the argument about faith in invisible realities.

last_rejected.why: οὐκ ἀντίῤῥοπα means 'not equivalent in weight/value to,' not 'counterbalancing'—the point is disproportion, not balance.
last_rejected.fix: not equivalent to our labors, but far greater than our contests
last_rejected.ruling: ἀντίρροπα means 'counterbalancing/equal in weight'; 'not counterbalancing' correctly conveys disproportion.

last_rejected.quote: the surpassing greatness of the dangers
last_rejected.why: ὑπεροχὴν means 'superiority, excess,' but here it is the dangers' excess over the prizes, or the surpassing nature of both; 'surpassing greatness of the dangers' misreads the comparison structure.
last_rejected.fix: the superiority of the dangers and makes a comparison of the prizes
last_rejected.ruling: ὑπεροχήν τῶν κινδύνων = 'surpassing greatness of dangers'; comparison with ἄθλων follows; no misread.

last_rejected.quote: more visible than the things that are seen
last_rejected.why: The Greek says 'more manifest/clear than the things that appear,' but the English 'more visible' creates paradox; φανερώτερα means 'more evident, more manifest to the mind,' not more visible to eyes.
last_rejected.fix: more manifest than the things that appear
last_rejected.ruling: φανερώτερα means 'more visible/manifest'; Chrysostom deliberately uses paradox; within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: You can see those things more than these
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἐκεῖνα δύνασαι μᾶλλον ὁρᾷν, ἢ ταῦτα
last_rejected.why: ὁρᾷν here means 'perceive, understand, discern' (mental seeing), not physical seeing; the English suggests optical visibility of invisible things.
last_rejected.fix: You can perceive those more than these
last_rejected.ruling: ὁρᾷν can mean mental or physical seeing; context of faith-vision supports either; not a clear error.

last_rejected.quote: lay hold of even the perishable affairs of this world
last_rejected.source_quote: τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ πραγμάτων τῶν ἐπικήρων τούτων ἅψαιτό τις ἂν ῥᾳδίως
last_rejected.why: ἅψαιτο means 'touch, lay hands on, engage in, undertake'—the point is undertaking worldly business, not 'laying hold of' in the sense of grasping or obtaining.
last_rejected.fix: readily undertake even the perishable affairs of this world
last_rejected.ruling: ἅψαιτο means 'lay hold of, touch, undertake'; 'lay hold of' is within normal range.

last_rejected.why: ἀπολαύει means 'enjoys, partakes of,' but the context shows the merchant endures storms for future trade profit; 'enjoys wealth' suggests present possession rather than anticipated gain.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπολαύει means 'enjoys'; after storms he does enjoy wealth—context supports this, not present possession only.

last_rejected.why: ἡ ἐμπορία means 'the profit, the gain from trade,' not 'the trade' itself; the unseen thing is the future profit, not the commercial activity.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐμπορία means 'trade/commerce'; profit is implied but 'trade' is standard; not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the reward is unseen, while the labor is clear and visible
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ μὲν μισθὸς ἄδηλος, ὁ δὲ πόνος δῆλος καὶ φανερός
last_rejected.why: ἄδηλος means 'unclear, uncertain, not yet manifest'—not simply 'unseen' but 'uncertain, not obvious'; the farmer's reward is uncertain, not invisible.
last_rejected.fix: the reward is uncertain, while the labor is clear and manifest
last_rejected.ruling: ἄδηλος means 'unseen/uncertain'; 'unseen' fits Chrysostom's visible/invisible contrast throughout; normal range.

last_rejected.quote: he will never even stir from his house
last_rejected.source_quote: οὐδὲ κινηθήσεται οἴκοθεν πρὸς τὴν ἐργασίαν ταύτην ποτέ
last_rejected.why: κινηθήσεται means 'set out, move oneself, go forth'—'stir from his house' is too weak; the Greek emphasizes active departure for work.
last_rejected.fix: he will never even set out from his house for this work
last_rejected.ruling: κινηθήσεται οἴκοθεν means 'stir from home'; 'stir from his house' is standard idiom; not too weak.
